To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the perceived validity of valence information can qualify explicit evaluations of social targets, and (b) the perceived validity qualifies implicit evaluations of social targets only when the validity information is presented immediately after the encoding.

the impact of perceived validity of object–valence contingencies on explicit evaluations is immediate and independent of the time delay, whereas the impact of validity on implicit evaluations is delayed and contingent upon the time delay.
the perceived validity (truthfulness) of evaluative information can qualify both explicit and implicit social evaluations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether implicit and explicit evaluations are based on different information-processing systems.
the question of whether people can be considered puppets on a string when evaluating social targets.

the impact of validity information on implicit and explicit evaluations and provides evidence that the two evaluation systems are not independent, as dual-process accounts suggest, but interact in a complex way.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the perceived validity qualifies both implicit and explicit evaluations, but only when it is presented immediately after the learning of the evaluative valence information.

the impact of contingency and validity information on implicit and explicit attitudes is not always as predicted by dual process theories, which assume that implicit and explicit attitudes are qualitatively different.
the perceived validity qualifies implicit and explicit evaluations, but that this qualifying impact is stronger for explicit than for implicit evaluations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the perceived validity and contingency of valence information are both critical for the formation of implicit and explicit evaluations, but the impact of these two factors on implicit evaluations is more sensitive to the timing of the presentation of validity than explicit evaluations.

the impact of validity on implicit evaluations can vary as a function of the temporal proximity of the presentation of validity to the presentation of valence information, whereas the impact of validity information on explicit evaluations is not affected by the timing of the presentation of the validity information.

the dissociations between implicit and explicit evaluations are not due to a parallel operation of two separate learning mechanisms, but instead reflect the impact of the perceived validity of valence information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dissociations between implicit and explicit evaluations can be explained by a single learning mechanism.
the impact of perceived validity on implicit and explicit evaluations is not necessarily parallel.
the perceived validity and the contingency of valence information are processed in a sequential, and not a parallel, manner.
